la:noun:merces.html:
merces, ēdis (
irreg. acc. mercem, ; Cons. Hon. 578), f.
mereo, what is deserved or earned; hence
, hire, pay, wages, salary, fee, reward, etc. (syn.: pretium, stipendium; class.).
Lit.: manuum mercede inopiam tolerare,the wages of manual labor,: ne ars tanta abduceretur ad mercedem atque quaestum,: operae,: veterum officiorum,: uti ab Arvernis Sequanisque Germani mercede arcesserentur,: haec merces erat dialecticorum,fee,: Apollonius cum mercede doceret,: mercedibus scenicorum recisis,the players' salaries,: poscere mercedes,to work for hire,: sarcienda vestimenta mercede certa accipere,.—Prov.: dignus est operarius mercede suo,.—
In partic., in a bad sense, an unrighteous reward, a bribe: pretio atque mercede minuere majestatem rei publicae,: magnā mercede pacisci cum aliquo, ut,: mercedem accipere ab aliquo, : lingua adstricta mercede,tied with a bribe,: iniquitatis, Pet. 2, 13.—
Transf.
A price for any thing, reward, wages; recompense, punishment; cost, injury, detriment; a stipulation, condition, etc.: mercedem alicujus rei constituere,: alicui proponere,: alicui rei imponere,: exigere ab aliquo,: merces sanguinis atque laboris,; : mercedem solvere,to make payment,: appellare,to demand payment,.—Prov.: unā mercede duas res adsequi,to kill two birds with one stone,: non aliā bibam Mercede,condition,: temeritatis merces,punishment,: qui metit mercedem accipit,reward,: in molestiā gaudeo, te eam fidem cognoscere hominum non ita magnā mercede, quam ego maximo dolore cognōram,price, cost,: non sine magnā mercede,not except at great cost,: victum illa mercede parare,: magnā quidem res tuas mercede colui,to my great disadvantage,.—
Rent, revenue, income, interest: mercedes Argileti et Aventini,: dotalium praediorum,: ex fundo,: mercedes habitationum annuae,house-rents,: publicanos tertiā mercedum parte relevavit,farm-rent,: quinas hic capiti mercedes exsecat, interest or discount on capital, .

senses: low salary, small wages, low reward
la:noun:mercedula.html:
mercēdŭla, ae, f.dim.
1. merces
.
Small wages, poor pay (class.): infimi homines mercedula adducti,: isto modo nec medico quicquam debere te nisi mercedulam dicis nec praeceptori,.—
Hire, rent, income: constituere mercedulas praediorum,.

la:verb:merito.gloss: to earn a salary or regular wage

la:verb:merito.html:
mĕrĭto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. freq. a.
mereo
. *
To earn, gain: vilicus, qui sestertia dena meritāsset,: Roscius histrio HS. D. annua meritāsse proditur,.—
To serve for pay, to serve as a soldier, be a soldier: meritavere Cato ait pro meruere, Paul. ex Müll.: Siculas meritare per oras,.

la:adv:merito.gloss: according to desert, deservedly, justly, justifiably, worthily, fitly
senses: according to desert, deservedly, justly, justifiably, worthily, fitly
with good reason, appropriately, correctly, properly, rightly, suitably, as a natural consequence

la:adj:meridianus.html:
mĕrīdĭānus, a, um, adj.
id.
,
of or belonging to mid-day, mid-day-.
(Class.) Tempus, mid-day, noon, : sol,: somnus,; .—Hence, as subst.: mĕ-rīdĭāni, sc. gladiatores, mid-day combatants, gladiators who fought at mid-day, .—In abl. adv.: mĕrīdĭā-nō, sc. tempore, at mid-day, ; .—
Transf., of or belonging to the south or south side, southern, southerly, meridional: ager spectat ad meridianam caeli partem,: pars orbis, opp. septentrionalis,: plaga,; : orbis,: circulus,the equator,: latus tabernaculi,.—Subst.: mĕrīdĭānum, i, n., the south, ; ; .—mĕrīdĭāna, ōrum, n., southern places or parts: in meridianis Indiae,.

la:noun:meridies.html:
mĕrīdĭes, ēi, m. (f. ap. ) [for medidies from medius-dies],
mid-day, noon.
Lit.: meridies ab eo, quod medius dies, Müll.: ipsum meridiem cur non medidiem? credo, quod erat insuavius,; ; P.: circiter meridiem,: ante meridiem, post meridiem,: diem diffindere insiticio somno meridie,to take a nap at noon,: inclamare horam esse tertiam, itemque meridiem, Müll.—
Transf.
The south: inflectens sol cursum tum ad septentriones, tum ad meridiem,: a meridie Aegyptus objacet, ab occasu Phoenices,.—
In gen., the middle of a given time (ante- and postclass.): noctis circiter meridiem, Varr. ap. : actatis,.

la:verb:meridio.html:
mĕrīdĭo, 1, v. n., and mĕrīdĭor, 1, v. dep.
meridies
,
to take a mid-day nap or siesta: jube, ad te veniam meridiatum,: meridiari ante cibum,: dum ea meridiaret,: inter acervos eorum meridiati sunt,i. e. have taken their ease,.

la:verb:merens.html: mĕrens, entis, Part. and P. a. of mereo, q. v.

la:noun:merx.html:
merx, cis (
nom. sing. merces, ap. P.), f.
mereo
, goods, wares, commodities, merchandise (class.): invendibili merce oportet ultro emptorem adducere: Proba merx facile emptorem reperit,: fallaces et fucosae,: peregrina et delicata,: femineae,for women,: esculenta,eatables, victuals,: navem mercibus implere,: sarmenta quoque in merce sunt,are an article of merchandise,: Arabiae et Indiae,: mercis sordidae negotiator,: in peculiari merce negotiari,.—
Transf., in gen., a thing (ante-class.).
Of persons: mala merx haec, et callida est,a bad lot,; ; .—Plur.: novi ego illas malas merces,: o mercis malae!.—
Of inanim. and abstr. subjects: ut aetas mala mala'st merces tergo! Ritschl N. cr. (in old MSS. for merx also mers is written acc. to Ritschl; v. Rhein. Mus. 10, p. 454 sq.).

senses: to serve, to render service to (with ablative of the person or thing interested)
la:verb:mereo.html:
mĕrĕo, ŭi, ĭtum, 2, v. a., and mĕrĕor, ĭtus, 2, v. dep.
cf. Gr. μέρος, μείρομαι, μόρος, etc.; hence, to receive one's share; cf. II. below
,
to deserve, merit, to be entitled to, be worthy of a thing; constr. with acc., with ut, with ne, with inf., and absol.
In gen.
With acc.: mereri praemia,: laudem,; : nec minimum decus,: amorem,: favorem aut odium,: gratiam nullam,; : fidem,: summum honorem,: supplicium,.—
With ut: respondit, sese meruisse, ut decoraretur,.—
With ne: mereri, ne quis,.—
With inf.: quae merui vitio perdere cuncta meo,: credi,: sanctus haberi,.—(ε) Absol.: dignitatem meam, si mereor, tuearis,if I deserve it,.—In a bad sense: meruisse supplicium,.—
In partic.
To earn, gain, get, obtain, acquire: quid meres? quantillo argenti te conduxit Pseudulus?: iste, qui meret HS. vicenos, Varr. ap. : non amplius duodecim aeris, Cic.

Rosc. Com. 10, 28: ne minus gratiae praecipiendo recta quam offensae reprendendo prava mereamur,: nomen patronorum,: indulgentiam, principis ingenio,: nomen gloriamque merere,: famam,; : ancillā natus diadema Quirini meruit,: odium,: quantum quisque uno die mereret,: aera,. —With ut (rare): quem ego ut non excruciem, alterum tantum auri non meream, would not give up torturing him for, etc., : neque ille sibi mereat Persarum montes ... ut istuc faciat, would not do it for, etc., .—

To get by purchase, to buy, purchase: uxores, quae vos dote meruerunt,: quid arbitramini Rheginos merere velle, ut ab eis marmorea Venus illa auferatur?what do you think they would take? for what price would they let it be carried away?: gloriam,: legatum a creditore,: noxam,: quid Minyae meruere queri?to have reason, cause,.—
In milit. lang., mereri and merere stipendia, or simply merere (lit., to earn pay), to serve for pay, to serve as a soldier, serve in the army: mereri stipendia,: meruit stipendia in eo bello,: adulescens patre suo imperatore meruit,: complures annos,: triennio sub Hannibale,: Romanis in castris,: in Thracia,: merere equo,to serve on horseback, in the cavalry,: merere pedibus,to serve on foot, in the infantry,: mereri aere (al. equo) publico, Varr. ap. .—
Mereri (ante-class., merere) de aliquo, or de aliquā re, to deserve or merit any thing of one, to behave in any manner towards one, in a good or bad sense (in Plaut. also with erga): te ego, ut digna es, perdam, atque ut de me meres,: ut erga me est merita,: nam de te neque re neque verbis merui, ut faceres quod facis,: saepe (erga me; sc. illam) meritam quod vellem scio,that she has often treated me as I desired,.—Esp.: bene, male, optime, etc., mereri, to deserve well, ill, etc.: de mendico male meretur, qui ei dat, etc.,: de re publicā bene mereri,: de populi Romani nomine,: melius de quibusdam acerbos inimicos mereri, quam eos amicos, qui dulces videantur,: de re publica meruisse optime,: perniciosius de re publicā merentur vitiosi principes,: stet haec urbs praeclara, quoquo modo merita de me erit,: Paulus, qui nihil meruit,i. e. was innocent,: ita se omni tempore de populo Romano meritos esse, ut,: Caesarem imperatorem bene de republicā meritum,deserving well,: optime cum de se meritum judicabat,: milites mirifice de re publicā meriti,: homines de me divinitus meriti,; cf.: te ego ut digna's perdam atque ut de me meres,.— Hence,
mĕrens, entis, P. a., that deserves or merits any thing; in a good sense, deserving; in a bad sense, guilty; that has rendered himself deserving towards any one or of any thing; with de, rarely with dat.; esp. with bene, well-deserving (mostly poet. and post-class.): consul laudare, increpare merentes,: laurea decreta merenti,: quem periisse, ita de re publicā merentem, doleo, ap. ; so .— With dat.: quando tu me bene merentem tibi habes despicatui,.— In sup.: HOMINI BENE MERENTISSIMO, Inscr. Rein. cl. 16, 8; ; .—
mĕrĭtus, a, um, P. a.
Deserving: meriti juvenci,.—Sup.: filiae meritissimae, Inscr. Rein. cl. 5, 35. —
Pass., deserved, due, fit, just, proper, right: ignarus, laus an poena merita esset,: triumphus,: iracundiam, neque eam injustam, sed meritam ac debitam fuisse,just,: mors,: noxia, committed, perpetrated, : meritis de causis, for merited, i. e. just reasons, .— Sup.: famā optimā et meritissimā frui,.—Hence,
mĕrĭtum, i, n.
That which one deserves, desert; in a good sense, reward, recompense; in a bad sense, punishment (only ante- and postclass.): nihil suave meritum est,: specta denique, quale caelesti providentia meritum reportaverit,reward, punishment,: delictorum,.—
That by which one deserves any thing of another, a merit; esp. in a good sense, a service, kindness, benefit, favor (class.): propter eorum (militum) divinum atque immortale meritum,: pro singulari eorum merito,: magnitudo tuorum erga me meritorum,: et hercule merito tuo feci,according to your merits, as you deserved,: pro ingentibus meritis praemia acceperant,: recordatio ingentium meritorum,; ; ; .—In Plaut. also in the sup.: meritissimo ejus, quae volet faciemus,on account of his great merit,: merita dare et recipere,: magna ejus sunt in me non dico officia, sed merita,.—Also demerit, blame, fault: Caesar, qui a me nullo meo merito alienus esse debebat,without any fault of mine,: nullo meo in se merito,although I am guilty of no offence against him,: leniter, ex merito quicquid patiare, ferendum est,: ex cujusque merito scio me fecisse,: quosdam punivit, alios praemiis adfecit, neutrum ex merito,; cf.: quod ob meritum nostrum succensuistis?.—
Transf., worth, value, importance of a thing (poet. and post-class.): quo sit merito quaeque notata dies,: negotiorum,: aedificia majoris meriti, of greater value, Cod. Th. 15, 1, 30: loci,: primi saporis mella thymi sucus effundit, secundi meriti thymbra, tertii meriti rosmarinus,.—
mĕrĭtō, adv., according to desert, deservedly, justly, often connected with jure (class.): quamquam merito sum iratus Metello,: merito ac jure laudantur,; cf.: te ipse jure optimo, merito incuses, licet,: recte ac merito commovebamur,: merito jam suspectus,; . —Sup.: meritissimo te magni facio, Turp. ap. ; : me deridere meritissumo,; ; S. C. ap. ; ap. .—Post-class.: meritissime, .—
In partic.: libens (lubens) merito, a form of expression used in paying vows; v. libens, under libet.

la:noun:mercator.html:
mercātor, ōris, m.
id.
,
a trader, merchant, esp. a wholesale dealer (opp. to caupo, a retailer; class.).
Lit.: venalicii mercatoresque,: multi ad eos mercatores ventitant,. —
Transf.
A dealer, speculator: non consules, sed mercatores provinciarum,.—Rarely of a petty dealer: vilis sacci mercator olentis,.—
A buyer, purchaser: signorum,: veneni,.

la:noun:mercatus.html:
mercātus, ūs, m.
id.
,
trade, traffic, buying and selling (class.): apud aedem Veneris mercatus meretricius,: turpissimus mercatus,: domesticus,.—
Transf., a place for trade, market-place.

market, mart: postquam pater ad mercatum abiit,: frequens mercatus,: mercatus conventusque Graeciae,: mercatu indicto,: Asiae Graeciaeque,; : (Numa Pompilius) mercatus ludos omnesque conveniendi causas et celebritates invenit,.—

In gen., a festival assemblage, public feast, transl. of the Greek πανήγυρις: mercatus is qui habetur maximo ludorum apparatu, totius Graeciae celebritate,: in mercatu Olympiaco,: Asiae Graeciaeque is mercatus erat,: magna pars Italiae stato in eosdem dies mercatu congregata,.

la:verb:mercor.html:
mercor, ātus, 1 (archaic form, mercassitur for mercatus fuerit, .—
Inf. mercarier for mercari, ), v. dep. n. and a. [id.], to trade, traffic, deal in commodities (absol., ), to buy, purchase something from a person (cf. nundinor).
Lit., constr. with aliquid ab or de aliquo, with abl. or gen. of the price (class.): aliquid ab aliquo,: fundum de pupillo,: aliquid tanto pretio,: hortos egregiasque domos,: quanti mercatura mullum luxuria?: hanc (segetem),.—In part. pres.: mercans, antis, subst., a buyer, purchaser: spem mercantium frustrari,.—
Trop.: ego haec officia mercanda vitā puto,to be purchased with life,: amorem muneribus, (3, 8), 15.—In pass. signif., to be bought (mostly post-Aug.): jam quidem facta emplastra mercantur,.— Part. perf.: mercātus, a, um, bought, purchased: commeatibus mercatis, ap. : cultus,: sestertiis centum quinquaginta milibus trullam unam mercatam a matrefamilias, (the better reading is mercatā matre, Jan.).

la:adj:merus.html:
mĕrus, a, um, adj.
root mar-, to gleam; cf.: μάρμαρος, marmor, mare; hence, bright, pure
,
pure, unmixed, unadulterated, esp. of wine not mixed with water: merum antiqui dicebant solum: at nunc merum purum appellamus, Paul. ex Müll.
Lit.: vinum merum, Varr. ap. : vina,.—Of other things: argentum merum,: undae,: lac,: gustus,: claror,clear, unclouded,: mero meridie,.—Hence,
Subst.: mĕrum, i, n., pure, unmixed wine, wine not mixed with water (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): ingurgitare se in merum,; ; : objecturus Antonio Cicero merum et vomitum,: meri veteris torrens,; ; : ad merum pronior,; .—
Transf.
Bare, naked, uncovered (poet.): pes,: stabat calce merā, Prud. στεφ. 6, 91.—
In gen., bare, nothing but, only, mere (class.): meri bellatores gignuntur,: in medio (foro) ostentatores meri (ambulant),: Diogenem postea pallium solum habuisse, et habere Ulixem meram tunicam, nothing but, only, Varr. ap. : nihil, nisi spem meram,: mera monstra nuntiare,: proscriptiones, meri Sullae,: scelera loquuntur,: bellum,: nugae,: adfectus,.—
Trop., pure, true, real, genuine, unadulterated: meri principes,: velut ex diutinā siti nimis avide meram haurientes libertatem, immoderate, excessive, Liv.

39, 26; cf. ; but mera libertas, in Horace, signifies true, genuine freedom, : Achaia, illa vera et mera Graecia,: Cecropis,a real Athenian,.—Hence, adv.: mĕrē, purely, without mixture, wholly, entirely (ante-class. and post-Aug.): si semel amoris poculum accepit mere,.

la:noun:merum.gloss: pure wine, wine unmixed with water, neat wine
senses: pure wine, wine unmixed with water, neat wine

la:noun:Mercurius.html:
Mercŭrĭus, ii, m., = Ἑρμῆς,
Mercury, the son of Jupiter and Maia, the messenger of the gods; as a herald, the god of dexterity; in speaking, of eloquence; the bestower of prosperity; the god of traders and thieves; the presider over roads, and conductor of departed souls to the Lower World: Mercurius a mercibus est dictus. Hunc etenim negotiorum omnium aestimabant esse deum, Paul. ex Müll.; ; ; ; ; ; ; sqq.: stella Mercurii, the planet Mercury: infra hanc autem stella Mercurii est, ea στίλβων appellatur a Graecis, ; so, stella Mercurii,; also simply Mercurius,: dies Mercurii or Mercuris,Wednesday,.—Appel. gen. plur.: Mercuriorum,—
Transf., the withers of draught-cattle, between the neck and the back (post-class.), ; .—
In partic.
Aqua Mercurii, a fountain in the via Appia, .—
Tumulus Mercurii, near Carthago nova, .—
Promontorium Mercurii, in Africa, in Zeugitana, near Carthage, now Capo Bon, ; .

la:verb:mergo.gloss: to dip (in), immerse; plunge into water; drown
senses: to dip (in), immerse; plunge into water; drown
to sink down or in, plunge, thrust, drive or fix in
to engulf, flood, swallow up, overwhelm
la:verb:mergo.html:
mergo, si, sum, 3, v. a.
cf. Sanscr. madsh-, majan, to dip; Zend, masga, marrow; Germ. Mark; Engl. marrow
,
to dip, dip in, immerse; absol. also to plunge into water, to sink.
Lit. (class.): eos (pullos) mergi in aquam jussit,: aves, quae se in mari mergunt,: putealibus undis,: Stygia undā,: prodigia indomitis merge sub aequoribus,: ab hoc (the sword-fish) perfossas naves mergi,: mersa navis omnes destituit,: mersa carina,: cum coepisset mergi,: in immensam altitudinem mergi, ac sine ulla respirandi vice perpeti maria,: naves,: partem classis,: pars maxima classis mergitur,: nec me deus aequore mersit,: sub aequora,; : ter matutino Tiberi mergetur,bathe,.—Poet., of overwhelming waters, to engulf, swallow up, overwhelm, etc.: sic te mersuras adjuvet ignis aquas,: mersa rate,.—
Transf.
To sink down, sink in, to plunge, thrust, or drive in, to fix in, etc. (poet. and post-Aug. prose): palmitem per jugum mergere, et alligare,to thrust, push,: aliquem ad Styga,: manum in ora (ursae),to thrust into,: mersisque in corpore rostris Dilacerant (canes) falsi dominum sub imagine cervi,: fluvius in Euphratem mergitur, runs or empties into, : visceribus ferrum. to thrust into, Claud. ap. .—Of heavenly bodies, etc.: Bootes, Qui vix sero alto mergitur Oceano,sinks into,.—
In partic., to hide, conceal: mersitque suos in cortice vultus,: vultum,: diem or lucem, of the setting of the sun,: terra caelum mergens, i. e. occidentalis, because there the sky seems to sink into the sea,. —Of those on board a vessel: mergere Pelion et templum, i. e. to sail away from until they sink below the horizon: condere,.—
Trop., to plunge into, sink, overwhelm, cover, bury, immerse, drown: aliquem malis,: funere acerbo,to bring to a painful death,: mergi in voluptates,to plunge into, yield one's self up to sensual delights,: se in voluptates,: mergit longa atque insignis honorum pagina,.—Esp. in part. pass.: Alexander mersus secundis rebus,overwhelmed with prosperity,: vino somnoque mersi jacent,dead drunk and buried in sleep,; ; cf.: lumina somno,: cum mergeretur somno,.—Esp. of those whose fortune is swallowed up in debts or debauchery: mersus foro, bankrupt, Plaut

Ep. 1, 2, 13: aere paterno Ac rebus mersis in ventrem,: censum domini,: mergentibus sortem usuris,sinking, destroying his capital,: ut mergantur pupilli,be robbed of their fortune, ruined,: mersis fer opem rebus,bring aid to utter distress,.—Of drinking to excess: potatio quae mergit,.

la:noun:mergus.html:
mergus, i, m.
mergo
.
A diver, a kind of water-fowl, Müll.: praesagiunt pluviam mergi,: mergi maria fugientes,; ; cf.: aequor amat; nomenque tenet, quia mergitur illo,; .—Jestingly: mergus agrarius, of one who is eager to possess lands,.—
A vine-layer, ; .

la:noun:mergae.html:
mergae, ārum, f.
root marg-, to clear away; cf.: ἀμέργω, ἀμέλγω, mulgo, amurca
,
a two-pronged pitchfork, with which corn, when cut, was made into heaps: mergae furculae, quibus acervi frugum fiunt, dictae a volucribus mergis, quia, ut illi se in aquam mergunt, dum pisces persequuntur, sic messores eas in fruges demergunt, ut elevare possint manipulos, Paul. ex Fest, p. 124 Müll.: mergas datus, ut hortum fodiat,: multi mergis, alii pectinibus spicam ipsam legunt,.—Comically: si attigeris ostium, jam tibi hercle in ore fiet messio mergis pugneis,i. e. a rich crop of fisticuffs,.

la:verb:merso.html:
merso, āvi, ātum, 1, v. freq. a.
id.
,
to dip in, immerse (poet. and in post-Aug. prose).
Lit.: balantumque gregem fluvio mersare salubri,: balneo infertur, calida aqua mersatur,.—
Trop., to overwhelm: rerum copia mersat,drowns, destroys,: mersor civilibus undis,plunge myself,.—
Pass.: mersari, to set, of the stars, ; cf. merto.

la:noun:Merops.html:
Mĕrops, ŏpis, m., = Μέροψ.
A king of Ethiopia, husband of Clymene, and reputed to be the father of Phaëthon, ; .—
A king of the isle of Cos, from whose name its inhabitants in early times were called Meropes, .—
A Roman proper name, Inscr. Mur. 887, 5.

la:noun:meretrix.html:
mĕrē^trix, īcis (
gen. plur. meretricium, : meretricum,; ), f.
mereo; she who earns moncy; hence
, a prostitute, harlot, courtesan: ita sunt hic meretrices omnes elecebrae argentariae,: meretricem indigne deperit,: proterva meretrix procaxque, Cic Cael. 20, 49: meretrix inter multos se dividit,: stat meretrix certo cuivis mercabilis aere,: Augusta, i. e.
